P2.s33.text: In the third quarter of 2026, TORM generated time charter equivalent earnings (TCE) of USD 353m (2025, same period: USD 236m). EBITDA for the Group totaled USD 274m (2025, same period: USD 152m including unrealized losses on financial instruments of USD 7m), while net profit for the period amounted to USD 199m (2025, same period: USD 78m). During the quarter, tanker freight markets were supported by continued disruptions to global oil trade flows stemming from the conflict involving the US and Iran. Following the collapse of the temporary ceasefire in July, increasing volumes of crude and refined products were exported from the Persian Gulf through shuttle tanker and ship-to-ship operations, creating significant logistical inefficiencies and absorbing substantial tanker capacity. Combined with constrained Middle Eastern and Russian product exports, strong export activity from the US and Asia, and a continued shift of LR2 vessels into crude-related trades, these developments supported freight rates at historically strong levels. In this market, TORM achieved fleet-wide TCE rates of USD/ day 40,102 on average (2025, same period: USD/day 31,012), and available earning days increased to 8,799 (2025, same period: 7,859). Our vessel class LR2 achieved TCE rates of USD/day 52,575, the LR1 vessels achieved TCE rates of USD/ day 38,667, and the MR vessels achieved TCE rates of USD/ day 36,137. | For the third quarter of 2026, return on invested capital amounted to 26.3% (2025, same period: 13.8%) reflecting the exceptionally high freight rates and basic EPS amounted to USD 1.94 (2025, same period: USD 0.79). Consequently, TORM delivered a strong financial performance in the first nine months of 2026, generating TCE earnings of USD 1,151m (2025, same period: USD 659m), EBITDA of USD 891m (2025, same period: USD 414m), and net profit of USD 660m (2025, same period: USD 199m). Business Highlights In the third quarter of 2026, TORM sold the 2007-built LR1 vessel TORM Venture and the 2008-built MR vessel TORM Laura. Following these divestments TORM’s fleet comprised 95 vessels, excluding vessels on order. During the third quarter, TORM continued to advance its fleet renewal and growth agenda. Following the acquisition of six MR resale vessels during the second quarter and the previously announced order of six MR newbuildings during the third quarter, TORM exercised options for an additional two MR newbuildings. Subsequent to quarter-end, TORM entered into agreements for eight LR2 newbuildings to be held through a 50/50 joint venture structure, and secured options for an additional two MR newbuildings. Collectively, these investments establish a significant pipeline of future fleet deliveries through 2030, reinforcing TORM's commitment to a modern and efficient fleet while supporting future earnings growth and long-term shareholder value creation. | Based on broker valuations as of 30 September 2026 of TORM’s existing fleet in operation (excluding the value of newbuildings not yet delivered), TORM’s fleet had a market value of USD 4,333m (2025, same date: USD 2,864m) and TORM’s consolidated Net Asset Value (NAV) was USD 4,062m (2025, same date: USD 2,401m) translating into NAV per share of USD 39.60 (2025, same date: USD 24.50). Coverage As of 28 October 2026, TORM had covered 53% of the Q4 2026 earning days at an average rate of USD/day 78,419. By vessel class, coverage stood at 68% for LR2s at USD/day 112,150, 38% for LR1s at USD/day 106,271 and 49% for MRs at USD/day 59,722. For the full year 2026, 88% of the earning days have been fixed at an average rate of USD/day 50,487. The remaining part of the earning days in 2026 - equivalent to 4,060 days - remains open and thus subject to market fluctuations. A change in freight rates of USD/day 1,000 will, all else equal, impact EBITDA by approximately USD 4m.

P2.s38.text: Market Developments During the third quarter, tanker freight rates rose to unprecedented levels as the conflict involving the US and Iran continued to materially disrupt global oil trade flows. Following the collapse of the temporary US-Iran ceasefire in July, increasing volumes of crude oil were exported from the Persian Gulf using dedicated shuttle tankers and ship-to-ship (STS) transfers in the Gulf of Oman. Crude flows from the Gulf increased further following attacks on Saudi Arabia's East-West crude pipeline, which prompted the redirection of volumes previously exported through the Red Sea port of Yanbu. Despite continued threats and attacks on shipping, the number of VLCCs deployed in shuttle operations is estimated to have increased to more than 60 vessels by the start of the fourth quarter. While this redirection reduced ton-mile demand for some Saudi crude volumes, as cargoes previously shipped to Asia via the Suez Canal and around the Cape of Good Hope were instead loaded in the Persian Gulf, this was more than offset by the significant inefficiencies created by the shuttle and STS system. By the end of September, approximately 14m b/d of crude was transiting the Persian Gulf, only 13% below pre-conflict levels and sharply higher than less than 2m b/d in May. The combination of recovering crude flows and significant logistical inefficiencies drove crude tanker rates to all-time highs, with the VLCC benchmark for the Middle East to Asia route breaking USD 1m a day for the first time in history. The recovery in clean petroleum product (CPP) flows has been considerably slower. Persian Gulf product exports remained below half of pre-conflict levels during the quarter, although an increasing share of the volumes that did move also relied on shuttle operations, involving close to 20 LR2 vessels. shuttle operations, involving close to 20 LR2 vessels. Repeated attacks on Saudi Arabia's Jazan refinery and the outage of the crude pipeline supplying the Yanbu refineries further tightened an already constrained global product | market, exacerbated by Russia's export ban following attacks on its refining system. Strong product exports from the US and Asia, particularly China, partly compensated for the loss of Middle Eastern and Russian supply and provided additional support to product tanker demand and freight rates. At the same time, approximately two-thirds of the LR2 fleet continued to trade in the "dirty" segment during the third quarter. This effectively reduced CPP-carrying capacity by around 4% compared with the start of the year, adding another layer of supply-side tightness and supporting LR2 earnings at levels significantly above historical norms throughout the quarter. Market Outlook Normalizing crude volumes from the Persian Gulf mean higher feedstock availability for refineries globally and thereby create a foundation for a rebound in clean product exports. This will support product tankers from already elevated earnings level. | Concerns over a potential US diesel export ban prompted EU countries to release 50m barrels of diesel from strategic inventories. In the near term, releasing inventories in major diesel-importing markets does not in itself create additional seaborne trade volumes or ton-mile demand. However, it helps mitigate the risk of demand destruction from exceptionally high product prices and supports underlying consumption. Importantly, inventories released today will ultimately need to be replenished, creating incremental import requirements and tanker demand once market conditions allow. The eventual normalization of Persian Gulf trade therefore does not necessarily imply an immediate normalization of the tanker market. In addition to recovering underlying oil demand, substantial volumes will need to be moved to rebuild depleted inventories across the system. The resulting restocking cycle could provide a meaningful additional source of tanker demand and ton-miles, particularly if inventories are rebuilt beyond the levels prevailing before the Iran conflict.

No 10-Q or reported 2026 IFRS revenue is in the packet; the 9M 2026 figures are TCE, EBITDA and net profit only.
No guidance gives 2027 or later revenue or margins. How long the disruption to Persian Gulf trade flows will keep freight rates elevated is not known from the evidence.
The capital cost of the newbuilding orders, including the eight LR2 newbuildings in the 50/50 joint venture, is not quantified in the evidence.
